about: Photo look with real NASA, Hubble and Webb pictures: travelling outward to the edge of the observable universe.

scenes.narration: Start with home. Earth, rising over the Moon. Light makes that trip in just over a second.
The Sun is about eight light minutes away. A hundred and nine Earths would fit across its face.
Our galaxy, the Milky Way, is about a hundred thousand light years across. It holds hundreds of billions of stars, and the Sun is just one of them.

image.credit: NASA, ESA, J. Dalcanton (University of Washington, USA), B. F. Williams (University of Washington, USA), L. C. Johnson (University of Washington, USA), the PHAT team, and R. Gendler (CC BY 4.0)

scenes.narration: Andromeda, our nearest big neighbour, is two and a half million light years away. On a dark night, it is the farthest thing your eyes can see.

image.credit: NASA, ESA, and S. Beckwith (STScI) and the HUDF Team (CC BY 4.0)

params.headline: A speck of sky. Thousands of galaxies.

scenes.narration: Hubble stared at a speck of empty sky, no bigger than a grain of sand held at arm's length. It found thousands of galaxies.

image.credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, and STScI (CC BY 4.0)

scenes.narration: Across the whole sky there are hundreds of billions of galaxies. Perhaps more stars than grains of sand on every beach on Earth.

image.credit: ESA and the Planck Collaboration (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO)

scenes.narration: The farthest light we can see is the afterglow of the Big Bang. The observable universe is about ninety three billion light years wide.

image.credit: NASA, ESA, G. Illingworth, D. Magee, and P. Oesch (University of California, Santa Cruz), R. Bouwens (Leiden University), and the HUDF09 Team (CC BY 4.0)

scenes.narration: Beyond that edge, nobody knows. The universe may simply go on forever.
And somewhere in all of this is us, on one small planet, circling an ordinary star.
